research.abstract: Background The 2026 cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome guideline broadens recommendations for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), but the increment over pre-2026 standards is unknown. We estimated the number and clinical profile of US adults newly eligible under this guideline. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of adults aged 30-79 years in the 2011-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Adults were newly eligible if they met 2026 CKM guideline indications but not pre-2026 American Diabetes Association, American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association heart failure, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes, or obesity guideline indications. Sensitivity analyses used 2 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label standards. Results Among 175.17 million US adults, 111.84 million (63.8%) were already eligible for either class. The CKM guideline added 7.48 million (95% CI: 6.48 to 8.47), a 6.7% increase, all for GLP-1RA and none for SGLT2i: 6.49 million with overweight (body mass index 27.0-29.9 kg/m2, ethnicity adjusted) and no other cardiometabolic disease, and 0.99 million with type 2 diabetes and 10-year PREVENT cardiovascular risk ?7.5%. Newly eligible adults (86.8% CKM stage 1) were younger (46.2 vs 52.9 years), leaner (27.8 vs 33.0 kg/m2), and at lower 10- and 30-year PREVENT risk (3.6% vs 8.1%; 11.3% vs 19.6%; all P < 0.001). Against FDA labeling, 14.15-25.17 million were newly eligible (7.66-18.20 million for SGLT2i). Assuming a 20% relative risk reduction, the projected number needed to treat per cardiovascular event prevented was 243 over 10 years and 56 over 30 years (ages 30-59) in adults with overweight, versus 61 and 26 in already eligible adults. Conclusions Relative to pre-2026 society guidelines, the 2026 CKM guideline newly confers a GLP-1RA indication on 7.48 million US adults, predominantly at lower cardiovascular risk. Whether treating these adults improves outcomes in a cost-efficient manner remains to be established.

research.abstract: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) may enable the extraction of clinically relevant information from unstructured electronic health records, but most previous work focused on identifying diagnoses without preserving their temporal context. We evaluated the ability of an LLM to extract diagnoses and associated dates from longitudinal clinical reports. Methods In an observational study using the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry, diagnostic annotations from 248 patients comprising 2343 clinical entries were analyzed. Six common comorbidity groups, subdivided into 32 hierarchical diagnostic categories, were evaluated. Using gpt-oss-20b, we extracted diagnosis presence, the number of diagnostic instances, and dates per instance. A reference standard was established through independent review by two physicians, with disagreements adjudicated by a third physician. LLM performance was assessed using diagnostic classification and temporal agreement. Direct annotation costs were compared. Results At the patient level, the LLM achieved an overall F1 score of 0.88 for diagnosis presence and 0.96 for the presence of a reported date. For the earliest reported diagnosis date, agreement with the reference standard was 86.73% at the day level. When considering the cumulative set of dates for each diagnosis, date recall was 87.63%, the extra-date rate was 20.88%, and full agreement was achieved in 58.19% of cases. Human annotators showed substantial disagreement in temporal annotation, with a date recall of 75.49%, an extra-date rate of 17.89%, and full agreement in 58.64% of cases. LLM-based extraction reduced direct annotation costs by 94.65%. Conclusions LLMs can extract diagnoses and their dates from heterogeneous clinical text with high agreement with an adjudicated reference standard. These findings support the scalable use of LLMs for longitudinal clinical registries.

research.abstract: Abstract Parasites can manipulate host behavior to increase their fitness while decreasing host fitness, a phenomenon known as an extended phenotype. Nucleopolyhedroviruses (NPVs), baculoviruses that infect Lepidopteran larvae, have been found to induce vertical climbing behavior and hyperactivity in exposed larvae. We quantified variation in the horizontal wandering behavior induced by different naturally-occurring pathogen isolates in the NPV that infects Dione ( Agraulis) vanillae Linnaeus (Lepidoptera: Nymphalidae). Lab-raised larvae were infected with a constant dose of one of five different field-collected NPV isolates or a water control (n=97 larvae total), and placed in mazes to measure the horizontal distance wandered away from a food source. Virus-exposed larvae exhibited increased maximum distance of horizontal movement compared to the control, but did not significantly differ in the probability of wandering versus no movement. We also found variation in the distance wandered among the five virus isolates. However, grouping the five isolates into two previously-described viral strains or genogroups did not improve predicted differences in movement, perhaps due to the presence of within-strain genetic variation among isolates in the viral genes involved in controlling host behavior. Further work is needed to determine whether the observed between-isolate variation is the result of adaptive evolution. These results suggest that the NPV infecting D. vanillae manipulates larval behavior to increase horizontal wandering, which could lead to higher pathogen fitness by increasing long-distance dispersal of the virus across the landscape.

research.abstract: Deep learning sequence to function models can predict the molecular effects of genetic variants, but their predictions are limited to the cell types and assays they are trained on. Here we describe DNACipher, a deep learning model that predicts the effects of genetic variants across diverse biological contexts-including those not directly measured. DNACipher takes 524 kb of genome sequence as input and predicts variant effects across 38,582 cell type/assay combinations, > 6 times as many contexts as AlphaGenome. We also introduce DNACipher Deep Variant Impact Mapping, a method to prioritize variants within trait-associated loci based on elevated predicted molecular effects relative to non-trait-associated variants. Applied to 590,604 common and rare variants at GWAS loci across 10 complex traits, DVIM identified imVars at > 90% of GWAS loci for 9 out of 10 traits. Common imVars were significantly concordant with statistical fine-mapping, and rare imVars were enriched for prior trait associations. For type 1 diabetes (T1D), imVars also had predicted effects that were supported by single-nucleus ATAC-seq, luciferase assays, and massively parallel reporter assays. DNACipher DVIM prioritises common and rare variants at GWAS loci by predicting molecular effects across cellular contexts.

research.abstract: Abstract Salticidae (jumping spiders) is the most species‐rich family within Araneae. Despite recent advances in phylogenomic studies, mitochondrial genome (mitogenome) evolution and its contribution to understanding phylogenetic relationships in Salticidae remain poorly characterized. Here, we present a mitochondrial phylogenomic analysis of 107 salticid species representing all seven recognized subfamilies. Using newly generated and publicly available mitogenomes, we investigated phylogenetic relationships and evolutionary patterns across the family, with a particular focus on comparisons between the highly diverse Salticinae and the species‐poor non‐Salticinae lineages. Our results show that the salticid mitogenomes are highly conserved in overall structure, with broadly similar genome size and nucleotide composition between Salticinae and non‐Salticinae lineages. Codon usage showed a pronounced A/T bias, with both mutational pressure and natural selection contributing to codon usage patterns. Phylogenetic analyses strongly supported the monophyly of Salticidae and all seven subfamilies in the maximum likelihood and Bayesian analyses. Lyssomaninae and Asemoneinae were recovered as sister groups, as were Eupoinae and Spartaeinae, while Onomastinae was sister to the clade comprising Hisponinae and Salticinae. Within Salticinae, Amycoida and Salticoida were recovered as major lineages, although relationships within Salticoida were unstable among analytical methods. Selection analyses indicated that all 13 mitochondrial protein‐coding genes are predominantly under purifying selection, whereas nad2 showed the most consistent signals of positive selection in Salticinae across the branch‐site, FEL and MEME analyses. Fifteen distinct gene rearrangement patterns were identified in Salticidae, including 13 novel patterns, with M5 inferred as the gene order of the most recent common ancestor of Salticidae. Gene rearrangements were more diverse in non‐Salticinae, particularly within Spartaeinae. Transposition was inferred as the predominant type of mitochondrial gene rearrangements in Salticidae. Overall, this study provides mitochondrial evidence for phylogenetic relationships within Salticidae and contributes to our understanding of mitochondrial sequence evolution, selection and gene order evolution in jumping spiders.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) transmission is sustained in part by asymptomatic disease states that limit the effectiveness of passive case finding interventions that rely on symptom-based diagnosis. Transmission models commonly represent the time spent with aTB using a single disease state, thereby imposing an exponentially distributed waiting time and a constant hazard of leaving that state. We evaluated how differences in the shape of the aTB waiting-time distribution affect the fit to observed disease progression data and subsequent projections of TB incidence and active case finding (ACF) impact. We fitted exponential and chained-state gamma formulations to cohort data on aTB progression and incorporated them into transmission models. The gamma-distributed model fits the data at least as well the exponential model indicating that the alternative model structures can also capture the changes of aTB cases. Comparing the fitted gamma-distributed model and the exponential model, we quantify how assumptions about the distribution of the duration of asymptomatic TB affect future disease trajectories and the expected impact of ACF interventions. Using India as a case study, we found that the gamma-distributed model projects a slower decline in TB incidence under the status quo, but a substantially larger reduction in the projected incidence of TB when ACF is employed, compared with the exponential model. These results suggest that estimates of ACF impact, and consequently assessments of its cost-effectiveness, may be sensitive to assumptions regarding the shape of waiting-time distribution of asymptomatic disease, indicating the importance of a better understanding of the natural history of asymptomatic disease for projecting of intervention effects.

research.abstract: Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is one of the fastest-growing epidemics associated with cognitive impairment and dementia. This reduces quality of life among patients with diabetes. Several trials on the management of cognitive impairment have been conducted, although their effectiveness and mechanisms are still unclear. Aim: To synthesize evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs examining interventions for cognitive impairment in T2DM, stratified by intervention category, comparator, patient characteristics, mechanisms, and clinical outcomes. Methods: We identified 11 systematic reviews (n = 213,604 participants) reporting the effects of cognitive impairment interventions through a comprehensive literature search. Using random-effects models, a meta-meta-analysis was conducted and heterogeneity assessed using I{superscript 2} statistics. AMSTAR and GRADE were used to assess the quality of reviews. Subgroup analyses were conducted for intervention category, cognitive severity, age, diabetes duration, sex, and follow-up duration. Results: Sodium glucose co-transporter inhibitors showed the strongest cognitive improvement effect (pooled OR = 0.44, 95% CI: 0.35-0.55; SUCRA = 94.5%), followed by GLP-1 receptor agonists (RR/OR = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.50-0.72; SUCRA = 92.1%). Among lifestyle interventions, multi-component exercise was the most effective (SMD = 0.69-1.04). The lower baseline cognition (MMSE < 23) benefited more from GLP-1 receptor agonists (Cohen's d = -3.00, p < 0.001). Advanced age ([≥]60 years) and prolonged intervention time ([≥]24 weeks for medications; [≥]6 months for exercise) were associated with greater effects. Female gender showed greater benefit from GLP-1 receptor agonists (HR = 0.63 vs 0.81 for male gender). Conclusions: SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists have the greatest effect on cognition in T2DM, and multi-component exercise is the most effective lifestyle component. The review therefore recommends individualized selection of interventions based on patient characteristics and baseline cognitive status. This calls for high-quality trials with prolonged follow-up to strengthen the evidence base.

research.abstract: We asked what topological structure adds to a clinical prediction model and how that addition should be measured. Drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) treatment outcome prediction is the testbed. The contribution is an evaluation design and a bounded null result. Cross-sectional records for 9210 patients from the NIAID TB Portals programme were collated to one row per patient by worst-case aggregation, giving a 99-feature clinical schema. We derived two topological representations. A Mapper graph, built on a UMAP lens over a Gower dissimilarity, supplied four neighbourhood-position features. Local Vietoris--Rips persistent homology on each patient's 26-point neighbourhood supplied degree-0 and degree-1 summaries, vectorised by the best of thirteen catalogued methods. We compared five feature configurations across four classifiers in a pipeline in which every topological step is fitted inside the training partition. A sealed test lockbox of 1776 patients, 463 of them with adverse outcomes, was opened once. We compared discrimination by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) using paired DeLong tests with Bonferroni correction (corrected threshold 0.0125). No topologically augmented configuration meaningfully improved lockbox AUROC over the clinical-only baseline under any classifier. The best AUROC was 0.7548, achieved by the baseline with XGBoost. Across all sixteen comparisons the upper 95% confidence limit never exceeded +0.014 AUROC. Five comparisons met the corrected threshold. Four favoured the baseline, and one, under the support vector machine, favoured the augmented model by a negligible +0.0005 AUROC.The same features supported neighbourhood-based risk stratification and revealed variation in adverse-outcome composition across patient neighbourhoods: adverse-outcome purity ranged from 5.9% to 30.5% across the fifteen largest Mapper nodes, stably under resampling. The findings support a complementary framing of topological data analysis in clinical prediction. Topological features are best understood not as replacements for clinical predictors but as an analytical lens that reveals geometric structure in the patient population not captured by the clinical feature representation alone.

research.abstract: Abstract Following the discovery of the piperazic acid (Piz)-containing hexapeptide demiguisin A from a toxic bird-associated Amycolatopsis strain, we aimed to investigate the structural diversity and bioactive potential of this natural product family. Here, we used the dmg biosynthetic gene cluster from Amycolatopsis sp. PS_44_ISF1 as a pathway mining probe to search for alternative demiguisin A producers. A global search identified only one other soil-derived Amycolatopsis sp. NBC_01488, encoding a highly syntenic pathway. Under feather-mimicking conditions, PS_44_ISF1 demonstrated enhanced growth and metabolite production relative to NBC_01488. Despite phylogenomic distance, both strains produced shared metabolites, while NBC_01488 yielded more abundant demiguisins, enabling the isolation of five novel derivatives characterized by two Piz-moieties with different hydroxylation patterns and glycine truncation. Two congeners displayed potent activity against the avian pathogen Mycobacterium intracellulare and moderate activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis . These findings show that targeted pathway mining guided the expansion of the chemical diversity of Piz-modifications and demiguisin congeners with promising anti- Mycobacterium activity.

research.abstract: Abstract The golden-yellow pigmentation on the body surface of adult large yellow croaker ( Larimichthys crocea ) is hypothesized to play roles in conspecific recognition, environmental adaptation, and visual signaling in natural ecosystems, while also constituting a key trait affecting its commercial value. In this study, we integrated genomic resources from eight species, including Sciaenids, and conducted homologous gene family clustering, phylogenetic reconstruction, divergence time estimation, and chromosome-level synteny analysis to assess genomic structural conservation. Furthermore, gene family expansion/contraction analyses, positive selection detection using branch-site models, and functional enrichment (GO/KEGG) were systematically employed to screen candidate genes and pathways associated with body coloration, alongside amino acid site comparisons and protein structural localization analysis of the candidate gene npc1l1 . Our results revealed that while the sciaenid genomes are generally conserved at the macro-structural level, the L. crocea lineage exhibits specific evolutionary signals related to golden pigmentation. A total of 11,470 shared gene families were identified across the eight species, with only four unique families in L. crocea . Phylogenetic and syntenic analyses confirmed the closest relationship with L. polyactis and demonstrated overall genomic stability among closely related Sciaenids. In the L. crocea lineage, 88 gene families showed significant expansion and 22 showed contraction; expanded genes were enriched in pigmentation regulation and lipid metabolism, yielding candidates such as cers2 , cers3 , hspa8 , and bax . Positive selection analysis detected 688 genes under selection, significantly enriched in intestinal cholesterol absorption, lipid digestion, and organic hydroxy compound transport, from which candidates including npc1l1 , npc1 , bscl2 , elovl5 , mc1r , edn1 , cd63 , bloc1s5 , and ltk were identified. Notably, among the two positively selected sites in npc1l1 , the 77th amino acid resides within the Niemann-Pick C1 N-terminus domain, suggesting a potential role in the adaptive evolution of carotenoid absorption. Collectively, these findings imply that the golden coloration in L. crocea may result from a combination of optimized carotenoid uptake, transport, and storage, alongside melanin regulation and optical enhancement mediated by iridophores. This study provides comparative genomic insights into the evolutionary characteristics of coloration‑related genes in L. crocea , enriches the molecular understanding of fish pigmentation mechanisms, and lays a foundation for future research and selective breeding targeting body color traits in this species.

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: In 2023, an estimated 13% of worldwide deaths resulting from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) were due to drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). The World Health Organization (WHO) documented a dramatic, sixfold increase in the number of patients treated with 6-month all-oral (BPaLM) regimens, from 5,653 patients in 2023, to 34,000 patients by 2024, while also documenting an emergence of bedaquiline resistance in real-world cohorts and a lack of efficacy of BCG revaccination in the BCG-PRIME Phase 2b trial against sustained Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Concurrently, the M72/AS01E subunit vaccine trial completed recruitment (approximately 20,000 individuals) across five high-burden countries, 11 months ahead of scheduled completion date. The first randomized controlled trial assessing DRTB-HDT host-directed therapy for DR-TB in adults (metformin + dovramilast), conducted at five international sites, is entering the late-stage readout phase. This synthesis of data, covering the period from 2015 through 2026, across six different dimensions includes molecular mechanisms of resistance, novel antimicrobial treatment modalities, host-directed therapy, immunity associated with regulatory compliance, adjuvants to vaccines, and the clinical translation of vaccine candidates. The Molecular-to-Translational continuum is used as a framework for the synthesis, with the regulatory immune function domain (T regulatory cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and check-point axes) linking all five domains. Our central hypothesis is that drug resistance evolution of the microbe and failure of the host to maintain regulatory immunity are interdependent and create a bidirectional relationship with each other. We have identified nine major research gaps, with milestone dates from 2026 to 2030, based on unresolved controversies regarding the bedaquiline resistance catalog and the acquisition versus transmission narrative.

research.abstract: The increasing prevalence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) and nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) underscores the need for novel strategies. Mycobacteriophages are attracting growing interest for therapeutic and diagnostic applications. Here, we describe four new subcluster A3 phages (Cat, Goose1D, Goose1X, and Shep) and investigate their genomic diversity and lytic activity. The phages share >98% nucleotide identity with known A3 members but carry distinct deletions within the lysogeny module: Cat and Goose1X have different repressor-loss variants, and Goose1D lacks the integrase gene, whereas Shep retains an intact module. All phages lysed M. tuberculosis H37Rv, with efficiencies of plating (EOPs) of 10 -2 -10 -1, but showed limited activity against NTM. Cat was the most effective against drug-resistant Mtb isolates (EOPs of 10 -1 -1), remained stable across a broad pH and temperature range, but had a low burst size (8 PFU (plaque-forming units/cell). In lysogeny assays, 6% of Cat-exposed M. smegmatis colonies exhibited a lysogen-like phenotype, but no phage DNA was detected, suggesting spontaneous resistance. Sequencing of one strain revealed an H535Q substitution in the pyruvate carboxylase MSMEG_2412. These findings highlight lysogeny module plasticity in closely related phages and position Cat, with its naturally occurring repressor deletion and potent lytic activity, as a promising candidate against drug-resistant tuberculosis.

research.abstract: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) assume additive SNP effects, yet genetic risk also arises from interactions between loci and environmental factors that contribute to broad-sense heritability. We developed an extended PRS (ePRS) framework for type 2 diabetes (T2D) that incorporates locus-by-locus non-additive effects beyond those captured by additive single-locus PRS or linkage disequilibrium (LD) tagging. These were modelled as interaction-informed cumulative burden (G+G; summed allele counts), epistasis-screened (GxG; allele count products), and gene-environment effects derived from cardiometabolic variables in electronic health records. Across 235,000 UK Biobank participants, five complementary ePRS models captured largely non-overlapping high-risk individuals, suggesting that a key to individual risk predictions comprises the inclusion of multiple interaction-driven biological components rather than a single signal. A composite score was predictive over traditional additive PRS and predictive of T2D among individuals whose clinical symptoms fall within normal ranges.

research.abstract: Diabetes screening can alter both clinical care and patient behavior, but its consequences for health and socioeconomic outcomes remain uncertain. We examine these consequences in a fuzzy regression discontinuity design using electronic health records from the American Family Cohort (AFC) and longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Survey (HRS). In AFC, we find that the diagnosis discontinuity peaks at 13 percentage points within six months and attenuates until it becomes insignificant at 42 months. We find a smaller and shorter-lived discontinuity for related prescriptions. These discontinuities remain across alternative specifications. Apart from specification and treatment window-dependent improvements in weight, BMI, and serum glucose, we do not observe a pattern of sustained improvement in cardiometabolic outcomes as a result of diagnosis and related care. In HRS, the threshold induces reductions of 22 percentage points in working for pay and 20.6 percentage points in labor-force participation at the two year follow-up. We do not observe a corresponding change in retirement, suggesting that diabetes diagnoses may lead to respondents reducing work without retirement. These reductions remain after several sensitivity checks but do not persist beyond two years. These findings suggest that health screening for chronic conditions may temporarily reduce labor supply, making employment responses relevant to the evaluation of broader costs and benefits of screening. research.abstract: Many patients living with chronic kidney disease (CKD) may not have a clearly identified cause, which can be a barrier to targeted therapies. We assessed the assignment of CKD etiologies in the national Veterans Health Administration (VHA) electronic health record data, overall and by demographics. We identified regular VHA users aged 18 - 100 years with new-onset CKD based on persistent eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2 occurring 2005-2015. CKD etiologies were identified by administrative codes over 3 years before and after the incident CKD date. Etiologies were categorized as diabetic, hypertensive/vascular, obstructive/urologic, glomerular, cystic/congenital, and tubulointerstitial. CKD was considered recognized, but without etiology, if only a general CKD code was present. Logistic regression models assessed disparities by sex and race/ethnicity after adjustment for age, US Census region, and calendar year of incident CKD. Among 452,851 Veterans with CKD, 42.5% were assigned at least one etiology. Hypertensive/vascular (24.5%) was the most common. After adjustment, non-Hispanic Black Veterans and Hispanic Veterans were more likely to be assigned an etiologically-specific diagnosis than non-Hispanic White Veterans (OR 1.61 and 1.23, respectively, each p<0.001). Differences were greater at younger ages. Non-Hispanic Black Veterans were much more likely to be assigned a hypertensive/vascular etiology (OR 2.17; p<0.001), but both non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic Veterans were more likely than White veterans to be assigned diabetic and glomerular etiologies as well (each p<0.001). Women were much less likely to be assigned an etiology overall, and in all categories, compared to men (each p<0.001). Women were less likely to have CKD recognized even if etiology was not assigned. Overall, the assignment of an etiology for CKD is low among U.S. Veterans, particularly among women, possibly due to poor CKD recognition. Types of etiologies assigned differ by race/ethnicity, which may represent true etiologic difference or biased assignment.

research.abstract: Interdisciplinarity is an environmental state as well as an individual state. It refers to either a state of collaboration among individuals representing traditional academic fields or to a state in which an individual is proficient in how multiple fields think, communicate, and operate. In this work, interdisciplinarity is explored at the intersection of three academic fields: bioinformatics, chemistry, and HCI (Human-Computer Interaction). First, physicochemical property information is incorporated into codon substitution models at site-level resolution to provide a mechanistic understanding of how natural selection is constrained by such properties. Three PRIME (PRoperty-Informed Models of Evolution) models estimate the effects of property constraints--hydrophobicity, volume, electrical charge, alpha-helix propensity and beta-sheet propensity--at varying scopes. G-PRIME estimates the global effects of these five constraints across a sequence alignment, while E-PRIME captures episodic effects by estimating heterogeneity (K=2) within an alignment and then inferring property constraints for each class. S-PRIME estimates property constraints at each site in an alignment. The PREI (PRIME Imputation) method infers probabilities for 61 sense codon states at each site in an alignment based on S-PRIME, providing insights into how a site may evolve given evolutionary history and physicochemical constraints. PRIME models are compared with state-of-the-art methods such as CoRa (Conservation/Radical) and ESM-2 (Evolutionary Scale Modeling) using simulated and empirical datasets. Second, scientific communication for bioinformatics methods--specifically HyPhy (Hypothesis testing using Phylogenies), which models nucleotide sequence evolution--is investigated using concepts from HCI. The affordances of both traditional and GenAI (generative artificial intelligence) e-tutorials are examined across three studies. In Study 1, traditional e-tutorials from 22 representative bioinformatics software tools were collected and analyzed using quantitative and qualitative content analysis. These e-tutorials are not merely step-by-step guides: they are well-grounded, particularly in computer science, and serve as key resources for communication and collaboration. In Study 2, the potential of GenAI e-tutorials was explored through an autoethnographic approach. The autoethnographer identified how information-seeking behaviors with GenAI can be described using the conceptual frameworks of orienteering and information scent. In Study 3, information-seeking behaviors using traditional and retrieval-augmented GenAI (RAG) e-tutorials were compared under the orienteering framework. Data were collected from 10 participants through lab studies, surveys, and interviews. The exploring search state was observed only in the RAG e-tutorial group, likely due to an increased sense of latitude. Harnessing interdisciplinarity pushes the boundaries of scientific inquiry. The contributions of the work are methodological, empirical, artifact-based, and opinion-based. The holistic value of interdisciplinary research is evident, underscoring the further need for collaboration across fields and for improving such collaboration.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding the minimal genetic changes underlying the earliest stages of speciation remains a central challenge in evolutionary biology. However, most model systems used to study early speciation involve pronounced ecological divergence, making it difficult to isolate the initial genetic changes associated with speciation. Here, we examined genetic differences between the cryptic cricket species Loxoblemmus campestris and L. sylvestris , which inhabit the same geographic region without pronounced ecological or morphological divergence. Despite their morphological similarity, the two species exhibited small but consistent molecular phylogenetic divergence in both mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. To investigate genetic divergence between these species, we conducted population genomic and comparative genomic analyses. We identified amino acid substitutions that were common within each species across orthologous genes and evaluated their evolutionary probabilities ( EP s) based on sequence conservation across Orthoptera. Although low EP amino acid substitutions occurred in multiple genes, three genes— Raf , Slit , and Sur‐8 —contained multiple such substitutions, and all three also showed elevated F ST values. These genes are functionally connected within the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway. These findings suggest that genetic divergence between L. campestris and L. sylvestris may involve changes concentrated in a limited number of functionally connected genes despite relatively few amino acid substitutions and limited phenotypic differentiation. Cryptic Loxoblemmus species may therefore provide useful systems for investigating early genomic divergence associated with speciation in the absence of pronounced phenotypic divergence.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT BACKGROUND Indigenous tribes face a disproportionately high tuberculosis (TB) burden due to deep-rooted socioeconomic disadvantage, highlighting the need for strengthened surveillance and control strategies. METHODS We conducted a 21-year retrospective study (2005-2025) among tribal and neighboring non-tribal populations attending a tribal-serving hospital in Karnataka. Pre-Nikshay data were transcribed from paper registers, and post-Nikshay data were obtained from the digital system. We assessed negative binomial interrupted time-series regression model, data completeness, TB risk factors, and used multivariable logistic regression to identify determinants of poor treatment outcomes and household contact screening yield. RESULTS We analyzed 1,512 TB cases (tribal = 1,021; non-tribal = 491). TB detection increased significantly over time, with a steeper rise among tribal populations (p<0.001). Nikshay implementation significantly improved data completeness (Wilcoxon W = 9900, p<0.001). Among tribal patients, males had higher odds of poor treatment outcome (aOR 2.81, 95% CI 1.70–4.85; p <0.001). Diabetes (aOR 2.10, 95% CI 1.05–4.03; p =0.029) was independently associated with poor treatment outcome. Among 503 index cases, 1,535 household contacts were identified and 1,161 (75.6%) screened; coverage was lower among tribal contacts (69.8% vs 87.2%; p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS Nikshay strengthened TB surveillance and improved assessment of TB burden and risk factors in tribal communities.

research.abstract: Abstract When conducting genome-wide association studies, addressing medication status that is relevant to the trait of interest can prevent biases that could distort estimates of the true genetic effect. Here, we introduce the genetic empirical medication reduction adjustment (GEMRA) method which uses a heuristic search for an empirical adjustment to be applied to phenotypic values of participants reporting medication use. Through simulations we show that the direct genetic effect estimates in the GEMRA approach exhibited less bias and greater statistical power than common strategies such as including medication as a covariate, restricting the sample to unmedicated users or including all samples without adjustment. We then applied the GEMRA approach to estimate statin medication adjustment for analysis of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels and antihypertensive medication adjustment for analyses of systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) blood pressure using multi-population data from UK Biobank and the Uganda Genome Resource. We found that a relative rather than an absolute adjustment better modelled the effect of medication on LDL cholesterol, SBP and DBP, with an effect of 40%, 10% and 10% reduction appearing to be consistent across populations, respectively. We also show that spurious differences in medication effects across populations can arise when the effect scale is misspecified. Author Summary When studying how genetics influence health outcomes, it is important to account for medications that can affect the trait being studied. Otherwise, medication use may make genetic effects appear stronger or weaker than they truly are. Here, we developed a method, GEMRA, to account for the effects of medication in genetic studies. Using simulated data, we found that GEMRA was better able to detect true genetic associations than several commonly used approaches. We then used GEMRA to account for the effects of statins on LDL cholesterol and blood pressure medications on systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Using data from UK Biobank and the Ugandan Genome Resource, we found that medication effects were better represented as a percentage reduction rather than as the same fixed change for everyone. Our findings also showed that choosing the wrong way to represent medication effects (i.e. as a percentage reduction or fixed value) can create misleading differences between populations.

research.abstract: Abstract Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infects the gastric epithelium of approximately half of the global population, and is a well-known risk factor for developing gastric cancer. Despite the clinical significance of H. pylori infection, many genetic factors underlying host response to H. pylori remain unidentified. Moreover, although H. pylori infection has been implicated in a range of extra-gastric diseases, whether these associations share a common genetic architecture remains unclear. We performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of anti- H. pylori IgG antibody titers, a composite host phenotype reflecting susceptibility to persistent infection and subsequent immune activation, followed by gene-based and pathway analyses, involving up to 140,863 individuals. This included 56,967 individuals in the discovery phase and 68,211 in the replication phase from Japanese cohorts, together with an additional 15,685 from European populations in a cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We reveal significant associations between IgG titers and polymorphisms in the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) class II region within the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC), as well as genes related to innate immunity, including CCDC80 , NFKBIZ , TIFA , PSCA , and TRAF3 . Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses revealed directionally consistent associations between genetic liability to higher anti– H. pylori IgG levels and a range of diseases, including immune-mediated diseases such as type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto’s disease, atopic dermatitis, as well as quantitative traits like body height and weight. These genetic findings support the interpretation that host genetic determinants of response to H. pylori , particularly those mediated through HLA class II, form part of a shared immunogenetic architecture associated with susceptibility to multiple immune-related diseases.

research.abstract: Immunotherapies have shown limited efficacy in prostate cancer, largely due to its immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment. Hypersialylation contributes to immune evasion by engaging sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-like lectins (Siglecs) on immune cells, forming glyco-immune checkpoints. Although this pathway represents a promising therapeutic target, the distribution of Siglec ligands across diverse prostate cancer phenotypes remains poorly understood. Here, we utilised high-affinity engineered sialoglycan-binding reagents (HYDRA) to perform immunohistochemical profiling of Siglec-7/9 ligands across a panel of 40 LuCaP patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. Ligand expression was evaluated in relation to AR status and neuroendocrine phenotype. To determine the impact of androgen deprivation on the tumour glycome, ligand expression was compared between matched PDX lines grown in intact and castrated mice. Our findings reveal widespread but heterogeneous expression of Siglec-7/9 ligands across the LuCaP cohort. Expression levels were comparable between AR-positive adenocarcinoma models and AR-negative neuroendocrine variants, demonstrating that this glyco-immune checkpoint is maintained across distinct prostate cancer lineages. Under castration conditions, glycan remodelling occurred in a model-dependent manner. To evaluate these therapeutic dynamics in human disease, individual trajectory analysis of paired clinical specimens from the Movember GAP1-UTMA cohort was performed, revealing patient-specific responses that phenocopy the model-dependent glycan remodelling observed across the LuCaP lines. These findings support the sialoglycan-Siglec axis as a lineage-independent target and suggest that strategies aimed at disrupting Siglec-mediated immune suppression may be most effective when combined with androgen deprivation therapy to enhance anti-tumour immunity.

research.abstract: Abstract Aim Understanding how biodiversity is formed and distributed is fundamental to anticipating how populations will respond to ongoing climate change and conserving future diversity. Sea snakes are a recent marine radiation comprising replicate lineages separated by vicariance and long-term isolation among major Indo-Pacific ocean basins. This system provides a powerful opportunity for testing whether demographic trajectories are shaped by regional history, phylogeny, or geographic range size. We therefore compare the demographic and phylogeographic histories of fully marine sea snakes to evaluate the role of Pleistocene climate change in structuring biodiversity across major biogeographic regions, including the global marine hotspot of the Indo-Australian Archipelago. Location Indo-Pacific tropical and sub-tropical marine. Methods We quantified demographic trajectories using whole-genome sequencing and integrated these with a broad-scale phylogeographic analysis of genome-wide single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP). SNP sequencing used 652 individuals to investigate the phylogeographic structure of 20 species across the Indian Ocean, Southeast Asian and Australian West-Pacific biogeographic regions. Whole genome data from 36 individuals provided coalescent estimates of effective population size ( N e ) through time. These N e trajectories were then analysed using phylogenetic comparative methods to test the effects of regional history, phylogeny, and geographic range size. Results Distinct within-species phylogeographic structure was uncovered between the regions supporting vicariance across biogeographic barriers. N e trajectories in the last 200 thousand years (kyr) were more strongly influenced by regional history than by phylogeny or contemporary range size. Southeast Asian lineages maintained the largest historical populations and experienced the shallowest population declines compared to lineages in the Indian Ocean and Australian West-Pacific. These results are consistent with the role of the marine biodiversity hotspot centred on the Indo-Australian Archipelago (IAA) as a region of long-term population persistence and stability during Pleistocene climatic fluctuations. Main Conclusions Demographic responses to Pleistocene climate change are strongly region-specific across the Indo-West Pacific, reflecting variation in habitat persistence and connectivity among ocean basins. Over the last 200kyr, regional biogeographic history is a stronger determinant of demographic history than shared ancestry and species range size. Based on these patterns, we recommend a hierarchical conservation framework in which ocean basins represent primary management units, and within-basin genetic structure informs finer-scale spatial planning. Of particular concern are Indian Ocean lineages, which exhibit lower effective population sizes and face intense fishing pressure and habitat loss. In contrast, Australian populations maintain relatively high genetic diversity and may represent an important regional refuge under future change. The demographic stability of Southeast Asian lineages supports the IAA as a long-term centre of population persistence, but this historical resilience offers little protection against current pressures: shallow marine habitats in the region are heavily degraded and sea snakes are directly harvested for trade.

research.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) caused disease Tuberculosis (TB) continues to be one of the leading causes of mortality although decades of medical research has progressed. With the alarming rise in multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant strains, the effectiveness of conventional therapeutic regimens is being severely compromised. This mounting resistance not only diminishes the clinical success of existing drugs but also poses a significant health threat, underscoring the urgent need to develop innovative therapeutic strategies that can overcome resistance mechanisms and restore treatment efficacy. Recent research has revealed that Mtb relies on unique metabolic adaptations for its survival and persistence within the host, particularly through the shikimate pathway, the methylcitrate cycle and the glyoxylate shunt. These pathways enable the bacterium to synthesize essential metabolites, detoxify toxic intermediates and conserve carbon skeletons under nutrient deficient conditions. The enzymes involved in these pathways exhibit distinct structural and functional features that are absent in humans, making them highly selective as drug targets. Advances in structural biology, enzyme kinetics and computational approaches have facilitated the discovery of promising inhibitors derived from natural products, synthetic scaffolds and fragment-based designs. This review discusses the mechanistic insights, regulatory roles and inhibitor development efforts targeting key enzymes from these three metabolic pathways. By integrating biochemical, structural and medicinal chemistry perspectives, here in the potential of these metabolic nodes as underexploited yet powerful avenues for next-generation anti-tubercular drug discovery are reviewed.

items.title: Bacterial competence and genetic diversity: Implications for the design of diagnostics and vaccines.
items.summary: Bacterial competence and genetic diversity are key determinants of microbial evolution, directly influencing pathogen adaptability, diagnostic reliability, and vaccine effectiveness. Natural transformation, together with horizontal gene transfer and homologous recombination, enables rapid genomic remodeling, facilitating the acquisition of antimicrobial resistance, modification of diagnostic…

research.abstract: Bacterial competence and genetic diversity are key determinants of microbial evolution, directly influencing pathogen adaptability, diagnostic reliability, and vaccine effectiveness. Natural transformation, together with horizontal gene transfer and homologous recombination, enables rapid genomic remodeling, facilitating the acquisition of antimicrobial resistance, modification of diagnostic targets, and generation of antigenic variants. These processes are particularly prominent in naturally competent and highly recombining pathogens, where population structures range from clonal to panmictic, shaping responses to selective pressures such as antibiotic use and immunization. This review synthesizes current understanding of the mechanisms governing bacterial competence and their role in generating genomic diversity, with emphasis on implications for diagnostics and vaccine design. Case studies-including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Helicobacter pylori-illustrate how recombination-driven diversification contributes to serotype replacement, diagnostic escape, and variable vaccine performance. Emerging approaches, including pan-genomic target selection, high-throughput sequencing, CRISPR-based diagnostics, and next-generation vaccine platforms, offer strategies to address these challenges but remain constrained by genomic variability and limited global surveillance. We argue that integrating evolutionary dynamics into diagnostic and vaccine development is essential for sustaining effectiveness. Continuous genomic monitoring and adaptive design frameworks will be critical to anticipate and mitigate competence-driven bacterial evolution in clinical and public health settings.

research.abstract: Abstract Influenza A (IAV) is a major zoonotic pathogen infecting a broad range of vertebrate hosts. In this study, we focus on inferring the evolutionary history of a subset of novel IAV, isolated from New World bats, which use a non-canonical host receptor and infer their relationship to sialic-acid-binding IAV. Little is known about when these novel subtypes emerged and how selection has acted upon them compared to sialic-acid-binding circulating strains. The current state of the field is split on whether bats are natural reservoirs for a distinct yet low abundance IAV lineage, or if influenza underwent rapid evolution after a recent spillover from a species within its standard host range. By analyzing segment-specific phylogenies, we hope to clarify the evolutionary history of bat IAV. Our objectives are to infer the date of divergence of non-canonical bat IAV from sialic-acid binding IAV, identify patterns of selection acting on bat IAV compared to representative samples of sialic-acid-binding IAV to identify potential signatures of genome-wide adaptation, and finally to reconstruct ancestral state transitions to infer which host taxa preceded spillover into bats. To accomplish this, we analyzed each IAV genome segment independently using least-squares molecular dating, Bayesian discrete-trait ancestral host reconstruction, and branch-site selection tests. Our results suggest that non-canonical bat IAV diverged from major IAV lineages 100-200 years ago, supporting a deeper evolutionary history rather than a very recent spillover event. However, discordance among genome segments in inferred divergence times, selective pressures, and ancestral hosts indicates that bat IAV experienced segment-specific evolutionary histories. Together, these findings suggest that non-canonical bat IAV represents a deeply divergent lineage with a complex evolutionary history involving segment-specific selection and host-transition dynamics.

research.abstract: BackgroundBoth over- and under-antibiotic use pose major global health challenges, yet there is no consensus on how to quantify deviations from optimal prescribing or set evidence-based targets. We developed a benchmarking tool for inpatient antibiotic use and evaluated its application in 10 countries. MethodsWe developed decision-tree models to estimate expected empiric antibiotic use for 11 indications, based on the WHO AWaRe book for two age groups: 28 days to [≤]12 years and >12 years. We parameterised the models using country-specific antimicrobial resistance estimates in the 10 countries and cross-sectional Global Point Prevalence Survey (Global-PPS) case-mix data from 2021 for 10 countries and from 2015-2022 in a subset of five countries. We then compared estimated expected antibiotic use with observed empiric use (from Global-PPS) in defined daily doses for adults and days of therapy for children, across indications and AWaRe categories. FindingsIn 2021, among patients aged >12 years, in all countries but one, observed empiric Access antibiotic use, as a proportion of total antibiotic use, was lower than expected and empiric Watch antibiotic use was higher than expected. Similar patterns were observed in all countries but one in patients aged 28 days to [≤]12 years. The magnitude of discrepancies between expected and observed Access and Watch antibiotic use varied across indications and countries. The median observed-to-expected ratios of usage across countries ranged from 0.3-0.8 for Access antibiotics, and 0.7-5.3 for Watch antibiotics in patients aged >12 years in 2021. Temporal trends from repeated surveys from 2015 to 2022 showed little change in observed-to-expected ratios for Access and Watch antibiotics. InterpretationThis benchmarking tool uses Global-PPS data to quantify differences between observed antibiotic use and WHO AWaRe recommendations. Our tool can be adaptable to local guidelines, provides policy-relevant estimates of expected antibiotic use to support monitoring, procurement planning, and targeted stewardship intervention. FundingThis study is part of the ADILA project supported by the Wellcome Trust (222051/Z/20/Z). The Global-PPS is supported by bioMerieux. bioMerieux is the sole private partner of the Global-PPS and had no role or responsibility in the study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation or writing the report. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSMonitoring antimicrobial use and benchmarking observed against expected antimicrobial usage given local disease burden and prescribing guidelines has the potential to help optimise antimicrobial use. We searched PubMed on 3 August 2026 for articles published since 1 January 2020, using the search terms: (((Benchmark) AND (Expected)) AND (Antimicrobial)) AND (Hospital). Among 37 studies retrieved, we found eight that benchmarked observed antimicrobial use against an estimate of expected use in hospital settings for interhospital comparison, all of which were conducted in high-income countries (the United States, United Kingdom, Finland and Japan). A range of statistical approaches including indirect standardisation, risk-adjusted regression, and generalised linear mixed models were used to estimate expected antibiotic use. Notably, none of these studies estimated the expected use based on antibiotic treatment guidelines, drug availability and risk of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in the study population. Added value of this studyWe developed a novel tool for estimating expected empirical antibiotic use based on the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines while accounting for local disease burden, risk of antibiotic resistance, drug availability and patient severity. We developed decision tree models informed by the recommended empirical antibiotic treatment for ten common infection syndromes and surgical prophylaxis for hospital settings in the WHOs AWaRe antibiotic book. The models were informed by data from the Global Point Prevalence Survey (Global-PPS) to estimate expected antibiotic use by AWaRe category in both relative (as a proportion of total use) and absolute measures. These estimates were used to benchmark the observed antibiotic use in the same cohort. We then calculated observed-to-expected ratios to quantify the deviation of the observed antibiotic use from the expected use, given reported local disease burden, and demonstrated the utility of these ratios for monitoring changes in antibiotic usage patterns over time. The findings indicated that Watch antibiotic use was substantially higher than would be expected if the surveyed hospitals had followed the WHO empirical antibiotic prescription guidelines, and there were improvements in Watch plus antibiotic usage for patients with age >12 years over the study period. Implications of all the available evidenceThis new analytical tool could enable hospitals to assess deviations in empiric antibiotic use relative to the expected use in both absolute terms (e.g. measures in defined daily doses and days of therapy) and proportional measures (out of the total antibiotic use) by AWaRe category. This tool can also be readily adaptable to incorporate local treatment guidelines. By identifying specific AWaRe categories and clinical indications where observed use deviates most from expectations, the framework provides a new tool to support the prioritisation of targeted antimicrobial stewardship interventions. Moreover, this tool could be used to monitor antibiotic use patterns in hospitals over time and identify possible cost savings.

research.abstract: Abstract Left ventricular reverse remodeling (LVRR) is associated with favorable outcomes in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), but the prognostic significance of LVRR first documented beyond 24 months has not been fully characterized in patients with diverse etiologies. We retrospectively studied 213 patients with HFrEF (baseline left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] ≤40%) who underwent echocardiography at baseline and in two prespecified follow-up windows: 6 to <24 months (Follow-up 1) and 24–78 months (Follow-up 2). LVRR was defined as an absolute increase in LVEF of ≥10 percentage points and a follow-up LVEF >40%. Patients were classified as Early LVRR (first meeting the criteria at Follow-up 1; n = 84), Late LVRR (first meeting the criteria at Follow-up 2; n = 25), or No-LVRR (not meeting the criteria at either follow-up; n = 104). The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization, assessed from Follow-up 2. Over a median follow-up of 33.8 months, 52 patients died and 32 were hospitalized for heart failure. In multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, and ischemic heart disease, both Early and Late LVRR were associated with a lower risk of the primary endpoint than No-LVRR (hazard ratio [HR] 0.299, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.164–0.544, and HR 0.293, 95% CI 0.115–0.744, respectively). These associations remained significant in alternative models adjusted for diabetes mellitus, estimated glomerular filtration rate, or heart failure duration. Kaplan–Meier analyses showed better event-free survival for the composite endpoint and higher overall survival in both LVRR groups than in the No-LVRR group, whereas significantly better HF hospitalization-free survival was observed only in the Early LVRR group. The mean Simple-GDMT Score, reflecting guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) intensity, increased from baseline to Follow-up 1 in all three groups, but a further significant increase from Follow-up 1 to Follow-up 2 was observed only in the Late LVRR group. In multivariable linear regression, greater increases in GDMT intensity were associated with higher LVEF at Follow-up 2 (β 1.265, 95% CI 0.237–2.293). Late LVRR was associated with favorable clinical outcomes, and greater longitudinal GDMT intensification was associated with higher LVEF at Follow-up 2, although causal relationships cannot be established from this observational study.

items.title: Structure-informed evolutionary analysis of the meiotic recombination machinery
items.summary: Despite being essential for fertility, many proteins involved in meiotic homologous recombination have diverged rapidly. The evolutionary forces driving this divergence remain mostly unknown, in part because of challenges in accounting for the interplay of sequence changes with constraints imposed by proteins' structures and physiological roles. Here, we explore strategies to more sensitively…

research.abstract: Abstract Despite being essential for fertility, many proteins involved in meiotic homologous recombination have diverged rapidly. The evolutionary forces driving this divergence remain mostly unknown, in part because of challenges in accounting for the interplay of sequence changes with constraints imposed by proteins’ structures and physiological roles. Here, we explore strategies to more sensitively detect signatures of positive or relaxed selection by integrating evolutionary analyses with structural and functional information, using meiotic recombination proteins in four taxa—primates, rodents, birds and budding yeasts. By mapping selection rate estimates onto predicted protein structures, we characterized protein regions likely to have experienced positive selection. We further identified subtle sequence variation within protein domains that are well conserved generally because of structural constraints. To detect sequence variation masked by these constraints, we analyzed selection at structurally matched residues, comparing homologs across different lineages as well as between meiosis-specific and generalist paralogs. These approaches identified lineage- and paralog-restricted enrichment of non-synonymous substitutions that may indicate loss of functional constraints and/or adaptive innovation. Finally, we used cross-species complementation experiments in Saccharomyces cerevisiae to show that sequence variation in the pro-crossover factor MSH4 modulates recombination proficiency. We suggest that evolutionary plasticity per se is a key conserved characteristic of the meiotic recombination machinery. More generally, our approach provides a mechanistic framework to analyze protein evolution. Significance Statement Meiotic recombination—the shuffling of genetic material during reproductive cell formation—is essential for fertility across all sexually reproducing organisms. Paradoxically, the proteins mediating recombination evolve rapidly despite their critical function. We used an integrative approach combining evolutionary analysis with protein structure prediction to understand how and why these proteins change. By mapping sequence variation onto protein structures and comparing meiosis-specific proteins to their generalist counterparts, we identified regions likely experiencing adaptive evolution or relaxed functional constraints. Experimental tests confirmed that sequence differences affect function. Our findings suggest that evolutionary plasticity itself may be a conserved feature of the recombination machinery. This structure-informed framework offers a generalizable strategy for detecting functionally relevant evolutionary changes in other protein systems.

research.journal: New Zealand Journal of Crop and Horticultural Science
research.abstract: Badnavirus decoloratiovitis , commonly known as Grapevine Roditis leaf discoloration‐associated virus (GRLDaV), is a member of the genus Badnavirus (family Caulimoviridae ) and a double‐stranded DNA pathogen associated with leaf discoloration symptoms in grapevine. In this study, the complete genome sequences and molecular characterization of two GRLDaV isolates, TR‐B42 and TR‐I3, obtained from grapevine varieties in Turkiye were determined. The complete genomes were amplified in nine overlapping fragments and assembled into circular double‐stranded DNA molecules of 7084 nt (TR‐B42) and 6987 nt (TR‐I3), with G + C contents of 41.2% and 41.5%, respectively. Both isolates exhibited the typical Badnavirus genome organization comprising four open reading frames (ORFs). Conserved domain analysis revealed a DUF1319 domain in ORF1 and characteristic Badnavirus replication domains, reverse transcriptase (RT), RNase H, zinc finger, and aspartic protease, within ORF3. Independent intrinsic‐disorder prediction of ORF3 across the six globally available GRLDaV isolates converged on a moderate‐to‐high disorder window localized to ORF3 amino acids ~830–890. This same interdomain window overlapped directly with the single prominent recombination hotspot detected in the TR‐B42 genome at nucleotides 3600–3800. Quantitative dN/dS analysis showed that ORF1‐3 were each under strong purifying selection, whereas ORF4 exhibited relaxed purifying selection. Phylogenetic and pairwise comparisons showed that the Turkish isolates clustered within the GRLDaV group and shared 85%–90% complete nucleotide identity with isolates from Greece, Italy, Croatia, and Argentina, confirming their classification as GRLDaV. Building on previous analysis of GRLDaV genetic diversity and population structure in Turkish vineyards using partial genome sequences, this study presents the first complete genome sequences of GRLDaV isolates from grapevines in Turkiye.

research.abstract: Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) is recognized as one of the most economically significant transboundary pathogens affecting small ruminants. However, despite the increasing availability of whole-genome sequences, comprehensive global analyses integrating evolutionary history, phylogeography, and genome-wide lineage-defining molecular markers remain limited. This study investigated the global genomic diversity, evolutionary history, and molecular characteristics of PPRV using whole-genome sequences. A total of 212 temporally informative whole-genome sequences, retrieved from GenBank (between 1969 and 2025) representing all four recognized PPRV lineages, were analyzed using comparative genomics, Bayesian time-scaled phylogenetic reconstruction, and genome-wide candidate phylogenetic marker; single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis and codon-based selective-pressure analyses. The results demonstrated high genomic conservation across all genomes despite their broad geographic distribution. Bayesian analysis estimated a mean evolutionary rate of 5.07 × 10 −4 substitutions per site per year (95% HPD: 4.79 × 10 −4 to 5.35 × 10 −4 ) and dated the most recent common ancestor of PPRV to 1839 (95% HPD: 1829 to 1848) which likely reflects the ancestry of currently sampled viral diversity rather than the historical emergence of PPRV. Lineage IV, the predominant contemporary lineage, was further subdivided into four geographically structured subclades: A, B.1, B.2a, and B.2b. A total of 125 subclade-associated fixed SNP signatures were identified, primarily within the L gene, with most variants resulting in nonsynonymous substitutions. The overlapping P, V, and C coding regions underscored the complex functional consequences of lineage-defining mutations. Gene-wide dN/dS values were below 1 for all six genes, indicating predominant purifying selection, while functional mapping identified several SNP related amino acid substitutions within experimentally characterized antigenic regions; however, these substitutions were not supported as positively selected in the present analyses. These results provide a comprehensive genomic framework for understanding PPRV evolution and identify candidate phylogenetic markers for lineage discrimination to support genomic surveillance, molecular epidemiology, and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)-World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) Global PPR Eradication Programme.

research.abstract: Background: Optimising sampling frames for genomic surveillance of E. coli and Klebsiella may support interventions to mitigate bloodstream infections (BSIs), but approaches to estimating sample size and how these relate to bacterial population diversity at multiple genetic levels (strain/plasmid/antimicrobial resistance genes [ARGs]) are lacking. Methods: Using systematically collected, regionally-stratified, whole genome sequencing data from a 6-month genomic survey of English E. coli/Klebsiella BSI isolates (n=1,939; NEKSUS), we used Bayesian approaches to estimate the sample sizes required to capture genetic diversity at strain- (MLST, fastBAPS clusters), plasmid- and ARG-levels, using two diversity measures: 'coverage' (i.e. proportion of the bacterial population/plasmids/ARGs represented by features observed in the sample), and the number/proportion of unique features observed at varying surveillance sample sizes. Our method is available as a user-friendly R Shiny application, EpiSENTRY (https://01a0c3dd-90d2-e597-58a5-51391a468387.share.connect.posit.cloud/). Findings: Randomly sampling 1,400 E. coli/Klebsiella BSI isolates each achieved [≥]80% coverage of bacterial lineages and ARGs (i.e. capture features constituting [≥]80% of the population) at 95% certainty, but captured lower proportions of unique features (28% MLSTs, 59% fastBAPS clusters, 19% plasmid subcommunities, and 57% ARGs for E. coli; 49%, 87%, 50% and 83% for Klebsiella, respectively). Sample sizes required for 80% coverage of E. coli plasmid populations were higher than MLSTs (1,928 [95% CrI: 1,837-2,025] vs 1,351 [1,230-1,472]), while for Klebsiella, estimates were lower for plasmids (1,115 [1,052-1,181] vs 1,422 [1,331-1,515] for MLSTs). Lower sample sizes adequately captured 80% coverage of fastBAPS clusters and ARGs (649 [575-727] and 27 [23-30], respectively, for E. coli; 113 [84-145] and 83 [72-96] for Klebsiella), due to feature-specific frequency distributions. Klebsiella BSIs were more diverse than E. coli, with sampling 10.9% vs 3.2% of total annual BSIs in England needed to reach 80% MLST coverage. Plasmid populations and Klebsiella MLSTs were region-specific, emphasising the need for regionally-representative sampling. Interpretation: Bayesian analysis facilitates estimates of context-specific genomic surveillance sample sizes. Cost-effective targets for coverage require further optimisation.

research.abstract: Abstract BCG is a well recognized old generic drug that can mold the human immune system through Immune Training. Broad basic science studies support Immune Training, but formal randomized placebo control trials are frequently lacking for confirmation of human benefits. Here we report on a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial with up to 8 years of follow-up. The primary outcome was mean percent change from baseline in HbA1c. At year 5, HbA1c in the BCG group was reduced from baseline by 7.04% (P=0.0006) and at year 8 by 12.84% (P=0.0001), whereas HbA1c did not change from baseline in the placebo group at either time point. Longitudinal percentage changes in HbA1c from baseline using mixed model repeated measures analysis with a comparison of BCG versus Placebo arms was significant (p=0.0017). This shows durable long term improvements lowering of HbA1c only with BCG immunotherapy. Secondary outcomes were also significant. There was a statistically significant reduction in average insulin dose only in the BCG-treated group (P=0.024). Glycemic improvements occurred without recovery of C-peptide from negligible baseline levels, suggesting no pancreas contribution. Blood sugar values obtained from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) similarly showed BCG immunotherapy lowers blood sugars compared to the Placebo arm (P=0.0189). CGM data also showed BCG immunotherapy resulted in an up to 183.7% improvement over baseline in time spent in normoglycemia (blood sugar in the normal range of 70-99 mg/dL) (P=0.0391). A sensitivity analysis confirmed BCG specific reductions in HbA1c were robust and durable at least to Year 08 ( P<0.0001 ). BCG was safe. These finding support improved blood sugar control through immune training of metabolism without a contribution of the pancreas even after long standing T1D. Trial registration: NCT02081326 .

items.title: Common centromeric variation associates with molecular and complex traits in humans
items.summary: Human centromeres harbor extensive structural variation that has remained largely inaccessible to human genetics because their repetitive -satellite arrays are absent from standard reference and imputation panels. research.abstract: Abstract Human centromeres harbor extensive structural variation that has remained largely inaccessible to human genetics because their repetitive α -satellite arrays are absent from standard reference and imputation panels. Here we catalog 188,589 centromeric structural variants (SVs) from haplotype-resolved long-read assemblies of 196 Human Pangenome Reference Consortium individuals aligned to the telomere-to-telomere CHM13 reference. Resolving recurrent SVs into monophyletic components along centromeric haplotype phylogenies makes them imputable from pericentromeric ( = 0.407 vs. 0.065 unresolved). In 124 individuals with haplotype-resolved nanopore methylation, we identify 418 same-chromosome SV–CpG associations that form local hypomethylation-enriched domains in the centromeric region, most strongly for deletions. We also show that a truncated 113-bp monomer on chromosome 8 is associated with the position of the CENP-A-associated centromere dip region (CDR) in 151 individuals, independent of array length. Imputed into 630 individuals with expression and splicing data, centromeric SVs are associated with 141 genes, 14 of them new relative to the SNP-based cis-QTL analysis, including the H3K9 methyltransferase SUV39H1 . In 315,204 All of Us participants, we identify 170 associations between 61 SV predictors and 27 clinical phenotypes, including substance-related disorders and breast cancer. Our study brings a previously inaccessible class of variation into population-scale genetics and links centromeric SVs to centromere organization, gene expression, splicing and complex traits.

research.abstract: The Mutational Hazard Hypothesis (MHH) predicts that reduced effective population size weakens purifying selection and promotes transposable element (TE) accumulation. Because effective population size is difficult to estimate across broad taxonomic scales, body mass, generation time, and dN/dS are often used as proxies. We analyzed TE landscapes across 167 sauropsid genomes to test whether these proxies predict genomic TE proportion consistently across phylogenetic scales. All three showed strong scale dependence. Body mass was positively associated with TE proportion across clades, but this relationship broke down within clades: only snakes retained a significant negative Pearson correlation after multiple-testing correction, whereas the corresponding phylogenetically corrected slopes were not significant. Generation time showed a strong pooled association that disappeared within every major clade in both Pearson and PGLS analyses. The pooled dN/dS-TE relationship also disappeared after accounting for body mass and generation time in a structural equation model, with a robust within-clade association retained only in turtles. Lineage-specific TE dynamics, including LTR expansion in sea snakes, were not captured by these proxies. These results show that commonly used MHH proxies mainly reflect clade-level structure rather than consistent within-lineage mechanisms.

research.abstract: Abstract: Benzothiazole (BTA), a fused bicyclic heterocycle of thiazole and benzene units, has become a special scaffold for medicinal chemistry with a vast pharmacological profile. Structural modification at the benzothiazole core provides enormous flexibility toward rationalizing bioactivity in a wide range of therapeutics. Contemporary research is exemplified by benzothiazole derivatives as potent antibacterial agents, efficiently targeting multidrug-resistant pathogens by mechanisms like DNA gyrase inhibition and membrane disruption. They also exhibit multi-target-directed ligand- based anti-Alzheimer's activity by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase, monoamine oxidases, and β-secretase enzymes. In cancer, benzothiazole hybrids are found to be selectively cytotoxic toward different cancer cell lines, such as breast, lung, and liver cancers, and are generally more active than the traditional drugs. Anti-tubercular activity presents superior inhibition of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, including, Multidrug-Resistance (MDR) and Extensively Drug- Resistance (XDR), by novel hybrid conjugates and heterocyclic linkages. Additionally, benzothiazole analogues exhibit anti-inflammatory and anti-diabetic activity with cyclooxygenase, Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 (DPP-4), α-glucosidase, and α-amylase enzyme inhibitory activity. Structure-Activity Relationship (SAR) analysis consistently indicates that electron-withdrawing or electron-donating functions, linker type, and heteroatom position in modulating pharmacological activity. Recent patents reflect sustained innovation in drug design with the benzothiazole motif, and therapeutic applications exist in antimicrobial, anticancer, neuroprotection, and metabolic disorders. Overall, these findings place emphasis on benzothiazole derivatives as highly effective lead templates with immense therapeutic value, warranting further consideration towards clinical usefulness.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a significant public health challenge, particularly among displaced populations. These environments foster TB transmission due to overcrowding, poor living conditions, and inadequate healthcare access Objectives To compare the proportion of tuberculosis (TB) cases detected through screening among displaced populations residing in internally displaced persons (IDP) and refugee settings with that among the general population in Benue State, Nigeria. Design Quantitative observational study comparing TB screening and diagnostic findings across displaced and general populations. Setting IDP camps, refugee settings and general-community screening locations in Benue State, Nigeria. Participants A total of 1,938 individuals were screened: 1,143 in displaced settings and 795 in the general population. Participants were assessed for presumptive TB and underwent the applicable diagnostic evaluation. Primary and secondary outcome measures The primary outcome was the proportion of screened individuals diagnosed with TB in displaced settings compared with the general population. Secondary outcomes were the numbers of presumptive TB cases and TB diagnoses classified as bacteriologically confirmed. Results Among the 1,143 individuals screened in displaced settings, 128 presumptive TB cases were identified, with 46 confirmed cases (26 bacteriologically and 20 clinically). In contrast, only 3 TB cases (2 bacteriologically and 1 clinically) were detected among 795 individuals in the general population. The TB prevalence rate in displaced populations was 4.0%, significantly higher than the 0.4% observed in the general population. Conclusions The study confirms a heightened TB burden in displaced communities, emphasizing the need for enhanced screening, diagnosis, and treatment strategies.
